children: According to Sina Finance, UBS analysts said a nationwide U.S. grounding and flight cancellations over the following three days would pressure airlines’ fourth-quarter capacity, revenue, cash flow and earnings, while raising unit operating costs. UBS expects available seat miles to fall 0.5% to 1% below its prior estimate and unit operating costs excluding fuel to rise 0.5% to 1%. The three affected operating days represented about 3% of U.S. airlines’ planned fourth-quarter capacity, and UBS estimated that cancellations eliminated about a quarter of the affected capacity. Higher unit revenue from passengers switching to other flights is expected to be insufficient to offset losses from cancellations.

The grounding on November 13 lasted more than four hours—more than twice as long as a similar event in 2023 and the longest nationwide U.S. grounding since the September 11, 2001 attacks. Across the six largest U.S. airlines, average cancellation rates were 32% on November 13, 30% on November 14 and about 10% on November 15; average delay rates were 26%, 36% and 33%, respectively. JetBlue’s cancellation rates were 43%, 49% and 28% on those dates. American Airlines’ cancellation rates were not reported for November 13, then stood at 42% on November 14 and 19% on November 15. Southwest Airlines and Alaska Airlines were relatively less affected.

UBS expects U.S. airline operations to improve significantly from November 16, with cancellation rates returning to the low single digits or near zero. The disruption adds to industry pressures from fuel-price volatility, high labor costs and substantial capital spending.

title: UBS: U.S. Nationwide Grounding to Weigh on Airlines’ Fourth-Quarter Results, JetBlue Hit Hardest
